Sequential decoding infers a hidden state trajectory from a noisy observation sequence.
In its dynamic-programming form one maintains a \emph{cost-to-go} vector
$v\in\mathbb R^{S}$ over a finite state set $S$ and propagates it backwards through
transfer matrices $A^{(0)},A^{(1)},\dots$ by the min-plus rule
\[
  (A\otimes v)_a \;=\; \min_{b\in S}\bigl(A_{ab}+v_b\bigr).
\]
This is matrix--vector multiplication in the tropical semiring $(\mathbb R,\min,+)$, in
which $\min$ is addition and $+$ is multiplication. The Viterbi algorithm, shortest-path
recursions, sequence alignment and finite-horizon optimal control are all instances.

An \emph{exact} decoder at position $i$ uses the full remaining horizon; a
\emph{window-$b$} decoder propagates only $b$ steps from an arbitrary terminal guess and
decides. Truncation is cheap and low-latency but may err. Practitioners call $b$ the
traceback depth and choose it by simulation. This paper replaces the simulation with
theorems.

\subsection{Results}
We establish: (i) nonexpansiveness of tropically stochastic steps in the span seminorm,
and a uniform contraction to the matrix diameter valid for \emph{all} matrices;
(ii) an absorption theorem bounding the span after a window by the minimum diameter
inside it; (iii) a \emph{tropical noise floor} obstruction showing no geometric
contraction estimate exists; (iv) exact cylinder probabilities, a union upper bound and
a Bonferroni lower bound for the Bernoulli environment; (v) a correctness bridge showing
lossless truncation on good windows; and (vi) a two-sided cost--reliability trade-off
with matching converse.

\subsection{Related ideas}
The span seminorm is the tropical counterpart of the Hilbert projective metric, and
$\Delta(A)$ plays the role of Dobrushin's ergodic coefficient. A reader expecting a
geometric contraction rate on the strength of these analogies should read
Section~\ref{sec:floor}: the analogy is exact for one step and false for many. This is a
structural feature of idempotent analysis, where $\min$ is a \emph{selection} and the
averaging mechanism behind classical geometric mixing simply does not exist.

\section{Tropical preliminaries}

Throughout $S$ is a finite nonempty state set, $q=|S|$, and all entries are real.

\begin{definition}
For $f:S\to\mathbb R$ set $\tmin(f)=\min_{s}f(s)$ and $\tmax(f)=\max_{s}f(s)$. Here
$\tmin$ is the tropical sum; $\tmax$ is auxiliary.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Span seminorm]
For $v:S\to\mathbb R$, $\spn(v)=\tmax(v)-\tmin(v)=\max_a v_a-\min_a v_a$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:span}
For all $v$ and $c\in\mathbb R$: \emph{(i)} $\spn(v)\ge0$; \emph{(ii)}
$\spn(v+c\mathbf 1)=\spn(v)$; \emph{(iii)} $v_a-v_b\le\spn(v)$ for all $a,b$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) $\min v\le v_s\le\max v$ for any $s$. (ii) Adding a constant shifts max and min by
$c$: one inequality by termwise bounding, the other by evaluating at an extremiser.
(iii) $v_a\le\max v$ and $\min v\le v_b$.
\end{proof}

Property (ii) is why the span is the right notion of size: the decision rule
$\arg\min_a(u_a+v_a)$ is unchanged when $v$ is shifted, so the decoder perceives $v$ only
in the quotient $\mathbb R^{S}/\mathbb R\mathbf 1$, on which $\spn$ is a genuine norm.

\begin{definition}
For $A,B:S\times S\to\mathbb R$ and $v:S\to\mathbb R$,
$(A\otimes v)_a=\min_b(A_{ab}+v_b)$ and $(A\otimes B)_{ac}=\min_b(A_{ab}+B_{bc})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tropical stochasticity]
$A$ is \emph{tropically stochastic} if $\min_b A_{ab}=0$ for every $a$.
\end{definition}

Every matrix becomes tropically stochastic upon subtracting each row's minimum, which
shifts $(A\otimes v)$ by a row-dependent constant and hence alters no decision. Note
stochasticity forces $A_{ab}\ge0$.

\begin{definition}[Diameter; tropical Dobrushin coefficient]
$\Delta(A)=\max_{a,a',b}\bigl(A_{ab}-A_{a'b}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

Thus $\Delta(A)\ge0$, with equality iff all rows of $A$ coincide. Small $\Delta$ means
the step is \emph{informative} (the source state barely affects destination costs);
large $\Delta$ means \emph{uninformative}.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:basic}
If $A$ is tropically stochastic then $\tmin(v)\le(A\otimes v)_a\le\tmax(v)$ for all $v,a$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Lower: $A_{ab}+v_b\ge\tmin(v)$ for every $b$. Upper: choose $b_0$ with $A_{ab_0}=0$; then
$(A\otimes v)_a\le v_{b_0}\le\tmax(v)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Contraction theory in the span seminorm}

\begin{theorem}[Nonexpansiveness]\label{thm:nonexp}
If $A$ is tropically stochastic then $\spn(A\otimes v)\le\spn(v)$ for every $v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:basic} every entry of $A\otimes v$ lies in
$[\tmin(v),\tmax(v)]$; subtract the resulting bounds on max and min.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical Dobrushin contraction]\label{thm:dobrushin}
For every matrix $A$---with no hypothesis whatsoever---and every $v$,
\[
  \spn(A\otimes v)\;\le\;\Delta(A).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $a$ minimise $(A\otimes v)_a$ and let $b$ attain $(A\otimes v)_a=A_{ab}+v_b$. For any
$a'$,
\[
  (A\otimes v)_{a'}\le A_{a'b}+v_b=(A_{a'b}-A_{ab})+(A\otimes v)_a\le\Delta(A)+(A\otimes v)_a .
\]
Maximising over $a'$ gives $\tmax(A\otimes v)\le\Delta(A)+\tmin(A\otimes v)$.
\end{proof}

The absence of $v$ on the right is the essential point: one min-plus step forgets its
input down to level $\Delta(A)$, however large the input span was.

\begin{theorem}[Associativity]
$(A\otimes B)\otimes v=A\otimes(B\otimes v)$ for all $A,B,v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both sides equal $\min_{b,c}(A_{ab}+B_{bc}+v_c)$ at coordinate $a$. Formally: for
``$\ge$'', fix $b$, take $c$ attaining $\min_c(B_{bc}+v_c)$, and bound the left side by
$(A\otimes B)_{ac}+v_c\le A_{ab}+(B\otimes v)_b$; minimise over $b$. For ``$\le$'', fix
$c$, take $b$ attaining $(A\otimes B)_{ac}$, and bound the right side successively at
$b$ and at $c$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monoid of stochastic matrices]
If $A,B$ are tropically stochastic then so is $A\otimes B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Nonnegativity gives $\min_c(A\otimes B)_{ac}\ge0$. Conversely pick $b_0$ with $A_{ab_0}=0$
and $c_0$ with $B_{b_0c_0}=0$; then $(A\otimes B)_{ac_0}\le0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of the diameter under composition]\label{thm:diammono}
$\Delta(A\otimes B)\le\Delta(A)$ for all $A,B$; and if $A$ is tropically stochastic then
$\Delta(A\otimes B)\le\min\bigl(\Delta(A),\Delta(B)\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The $c$-th column of $A\otimes B$ is $A\otimes(B_{\bullet c})$, so any row difference of
the product is bounded by the span of that column. For the first claim apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:dobrushin} to the column; for the second apply Theorem~\ref{thm:nonexp}
and note that the span of a column of $B$ is a row difference of $B$, hence at most
$\Delta(B)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sup-norm stability]
For every $A$, all $v,w$ and all $a$,
$\bigl|(A\otimes v)_a-(A\otimes w)_a\bigr|\le\max_s|v_s-w_s|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $M=\max_s|v_s-w_s|$, so $v\le w+M\mathbf 1$ pointwise. The min-plus action is
monotone and satisfies $A\otimes(w+M\mathbf 1)=(A\otimes w)+M\mathbf 1$; hence
$A\otimes v\le A\otimes w+M\mathbf 1$, and symmetrically.
\end{proof}

\section{Windows and the absorption theorem}

\begin{definition}[Windowed propagation]
Given a chain $A^{(0)},A^{(1)},\dots$ define $W_{i,0}(v)=v$ and
$W_{i,k+1}(v)=A^{(i)}\otimes W_{i+1,k}(v)$. Thus $W_{i,k}(v)$ propagates a terminal guess
$v$ backwards through $A^{(i)},\dots,A^{(i+k-1)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Window composition]\label{lem:comp}
$W_{i,j+r}(v)=W_{i,j}\bigl(W_{i+j,r}(v)\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $j$, using the recursion and the index identity $i+(j+1)=(i+1)+j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:winnonexp}
If every $A^{(i)}$ is tropically stochastic then $\spn(W_{i,k}(v))\le\spn(v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $k$ using Theorem~\ref{thm:nonexp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Absorption]\label{thm:absorption}
Assume every $A^{(i)}$ is tropically stochastic. Then for every $j<k$ and every $v$,
\[
  \spn\bigl(W_{i,k}(v)\bigr)\;\le\;\Delta\bigl(A^{(i+j)}\bigr),
  \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
  \spn\bigl(W_{i,k}(v)\bigr)\;\le\;\min_{0\le j<k}\Delta\bigl(A^{(i+j)}\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $k=j+(m+1)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:comp},
$W_{i,k}(v)=W_{i,j}\bigl(A^{(i+j)}\otimes W_{i+j+1,m}(v)\bigr)$. The outer $j$ steps do
not increase the span (Theorem~\ref{thm:winnonexp}), and the inner bracket has span at
most $\Delta(A^{(i+j)})$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:dobrushin}, uniformly in whatever the deeper
propagation produced.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:absorption} says that memory loss in min-plus dynamics is not an
accumulation of small effects but a threshold event: one informative step anywhere in the
window caps the span, and the surrounding steps neither help nor hurt.

\section{The tropical noise floor}\label{sec:floor}

Given the preceding results the natural conjecture is a geometric estimate
$\spn(W_{i,k}(v))\le\rho^{k}\spn(v)$ with $\rho<1$, in analogy with Birkhoff--Hopf
contraction and geometric ergodicity. No such estimate exists.

\begin{definition}
For $d\ge0$ let $T_d$ be the two-state matrix on $S=\{0,1\}$ with $(T_d)_{ab}=0$ if $a=b$
and $d$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$T_d$ is tropically stochastic and $\Delta(T_d)=d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each row is $(0,d)$ or $(d,0)$, of minimum $0$; row differences take values $0,\pm d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:fixed}
$T_d\otimes(0,d)=(0,d)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Coordinate $0$: $\min(0+0,\,d+d)=0$ since $d\ge0$. Coordinate $1$: $\min(d+0,\,0+d)=d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical noise floor]\label{thm:floor}
For the constant chain $A^{(i)}=T_d$, every $k\ge0$ and every $i$,
\[
  \spn\bigl(W_{i,k}(0,d)\bigr)\;=\;d\;=\;\Delta(T_d).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed} and induction, $W_{i,k}(0,d)=(0,d)$; its span is $d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
There is no $\rho<1$ and no constant $C$ with $\spn(W_{i,k}(v))\le C\rho^{k}\spn(v)$ for
all tropically stochastic chains, all $v$ and all $k$. Indeed the absorption bound is
attained with equality at every window length.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Classical geometric mixing is driven by \emph{averaging}: a convex combination of two
values lies strictly between them, so iteration shrinks differences at a definite rate.
Min-plus addition is idempotent and \emph{selective}: $\min$ returns one of its arguments.
A min-plus step can discard a spread wholesale---that is Theorem~\ref{thm:dobrushin}---but
cannot erode a spread that no single step removes. Symmetric ambiguity is a fixed point of
selection dynamics and survives forever. Consequently the exponential reliability gain of
a longer decoding window cannot be an algebraic phenomenon; it must come from the
statistics of the diameters along the chain.
\end{remark}

\section{The Bernoulli environment}

\begin{definition}
An \emph{environment} of length $n$ is $\omega:\{0,\dots,n-1\}\to\{\text{true},\text{false}\}$,
where $\omega_i=\text{true}$ means step $i$ is \emph{informative}. Given a threshold
$\theta$ and a chain $A$, the \emph{induced environment} is
$\omega_i=[\Delta(A^{(i)})\le\theta]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
For $p\in[0,1]$ let $w_p(\omega)=\prod_{i<n}\bigl(p\,[\omega_i]+(1-p)\,[\lnot\omega_i]\bigr)$
and $\Prp[E]=\sum_{\omega\in E}w_p(\omega)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
The weights are nonnegative, total mass is $1$, $\Prp$ is monotone under inclusion, and
$\Prp[E^{c}]=1-\Prp[E]$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Distributing the sum over environments through the product over coordinates gives
$\prod_i(p+(1-p))=1$; the rest is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
For a position set $W$, let $\mathcal B(W)=\{\omega:\omega_x=\text{false}\ \forall x\in W\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cylinder probability]\label{thm:cyl}
$\Prp[\mathcal B(W)]=(1-p)^{|W|}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The sum factorises over coordinates as $\prod_{x\in W}(1-p)\prod_{x\notin W}(p+(1-p))$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:inter}
$\mathcal B(W_1)\cap\mathcal B(W_2)=\mathcal B(W_1\cup W_2)$, so the intersection has
probability $(1-p)^{|W_1\cup W_2|}$; for disjoint $W_1,W_2$ this factorises, i.e.\
disjoint coordinate blocks are independent.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}
With $\Win(i,b)=\{x:i\le x<i+b\}\cap\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and
$\mathcal W_{i,b}=\mathcal B(\Win(i,b))$, the failure event of the window-$b$ decoder is
$\mathcal F_{n,b}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{n-b}\mathcal W_{i,b}$.
\end{definition}

If $i+b\le n$ then $|\Win(i,b)|=b$ and $\Prp[\mathcal W_{i,b}]=(1-p)^{b}$ exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Union upper bound]\label{thm:union}
For $0\le p\le1$ and $b\le n$, $\ \Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le(n+1-b)(1-p)^{b}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Subadditivity of $\Prp$ over a finite union (immediate from nonnegativity of the weights),
together with Theorem~\ref{thm:cyl} applied to each of the $n+1-b$ windows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Elementary lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
For $0\le p\le1$ and $b\le n$, $\ (1-p)^{b}\le\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\mathcal W_{0,b}\subseteq\mathcal F_{n,b}$ has probability exactly $(1-p)^{b}$.
\end{proof}

Specialising $b=1$ gives $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,1}]\le n(1-p)$ (symbol-by-symbol decoding);
specialising $b=n$ gives $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,n}]\le(1-p)^{n}$ (full-block decoding).
Theorem~\ref{thm:union} is the exact interpolation between the endpoints.

\subsection{Closing the polynomial gap}

\begin{theorem}[Second Bonferroni inequality]\label{thm:bonf}
For events $E_0,\dots,E_{m-1}$,
\[
  \sum_{i<m}\Prp[E_i]-\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<i}\Prp[E_j\cap E_i]\;\le\;\Prp\Bigl[\bigcup_{i<m}E_i\Bigr].
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $m$, using inclusion--exclusion for two events,
$\Prp[E_m\cup U]+\Prp[E_m\cap U]=\Prp[E_m]+\Prp[U]$ with $U=\bigcup_{i<m}E_i$, together
with subadditivity $\Prp[E_m\cap U]\le\sum_{j<m}\Prp[E_j\cap E_m]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bonferroni lower bound]\label{thm:bonflower}
If $mb\le n$ then
$\ m(1-p)^{b}-\frac{m(m-1)}{2}(1-p)^{2b}\le\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:bonf} to the pairwise disjoint windows
$E_t=\mathcal W_{tb,b}$, $t<m$. Each has probability $(1-p)^{b}$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyl}; each of the $\binom m2$ pairwise intersections has probability
$(1-p)^{2b}$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:inter}. Finally
$\bigcup_t E_t\subseteq\mathcal F_{n,b}$ and $\Prp$ is monotone.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:half}
If $mb\le n$ and $m(1-p)^{b}\le1$ then $\ \frac m2(1-p)^{b}\le\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
With $x=(1-p)^{b}$, $\frac{m(m-1)}2x^{2}\le\frac m2(mx)x\le\frac m2x$ since $mx\le1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:sandwichprob}
With $m=\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ and $m(1-p)^{b}\le1$,
\[
  \frac{\lfloor n/b\rfloor}{2}(1-p)^{b}\;\le\;\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\;\le\;(n+1-b)(1-p)^{b},
\]
so the two bounds differ by a factor at most $\approx2b$, down from $\approx n$.
\end{corollary}

\section{The correctness bridge}

\begin{definition}
Given a local cost $u$ and a cost-to-go vector $V$, a state $a_0$ \emph{is a decision} if
$u_{a_0}+V_{a_0}\le u_a+V_a$ for all $a$, and \emph{wins by margin $m$} if
$u_{a_0}+V_{a_0}+m\le u_a+V_a$ for all $a\ne a_0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Robustness of margins]\label{thm:robust}
Let $\theta\ge0$, let $\spn(V)\le\theta$ and $\spn(W)\le\theta$, and suppose $a_0$ wins by
margin $2\theta$ with respect to $W$. Then $a_0$ is a decision with respect to $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $a\ne a_0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:span}(iii), $V_{a_0}-V_a\le\theta$ and
$W_a-W_{a_0}\le\theta$; with $u_{a_0}+W_{a_0}+2\theta\le u_a+W_a$ these combine linearly
to $u_{a_0}+V_{a_0}\le u_a+V_a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Lossless truncation]\label{thm:locality}
Assume every $A^{(i)}$ is tropically stochastic. Suppose some $j<b$ has
$\Delta(A^{(i+j)})\le\theta$, and that the window-$b$ decision $a_0$ computed from a
terminal guess $w$ wins by margin $2\theta$ against $W_{i,b}(w)$. Then for every $r\ge0$
and every terminal guess $v$, $a_0$ is a decision for $W_{i,b+r}(v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both windows contain index $j$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:absorption} both $W_{i,b}(w)$ and
$W_{i,b+r}(v)$ have span at most $\Delta(A^{(i+j)})\le\theta$; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:robust}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Correctness on good environments]
Assume every $A^{(i)}$ is tropically stochastic and let $\omega$ be the environment
induced at threshold $\theta$. If $\omega\notin\mathcal F_{n,b}$ then the conclusion of
Theorem~\ref{thm:locality} holds at every position $i$ with $i+b\le n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\omega\notin\mathcal W_{i,b}$ gives some $j<b$ with $\Delta(A^{(i+j)})\le\theta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For $b\le n$, the set of environments on which the window-$b$ decoder is lossless at every
admissible position has probability at least $1-(n+1-b)(1-p)^{b}$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Cost model, converse, and achievability}

\begin{definition}
One min-plus matrix--vector product on $q=|S|$ states costs $q^{2}$ scalar operations, so
the horizon-$k$ recursion costs $kq^{2}$ and the window-$b$ decoder over $n$ positions
costs $C(b)=nbq^{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$C(1)=nq^{2}$; $C(n)=n^{2}q^{2}$; $C(b)=b\,C(1)$; $C(1)\le C(b)\le C(n)$ for
$1\le b\le n$; and $C$ is strictly increasing in $b$ when $q,n\ge1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Converse: reliability exponent]\label{thm:conv}
For $0\le p<1$ and $b\le n$,
$\ \log\bigl(1/\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\bigr)\le b\log\frac1{1-p}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\ge(1-p)^{b}>0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:lower}; take logarithms and
negate.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Window and cost lower bounds]
Let $0<p<1$, $b\le n$, and $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le\varepsilon$. Then
\[
  b\;\ge\;\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\frac1{1-p}},
  \qquad
  nq^{2}\cdot\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\frac1{1-p}}\;\le\;C(b).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$(1-p)^{b}\le\varepsilon$ gives the first; multiply by $nq^{2}\ge0$ and use $C(b)=nq^{2}b$
for the second.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Trade-off invariant]
For $0\le p<1$ and $b\le n$,
\[
  \log\frac{1}{\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]}\cdot\bigl(nq^{2}\bigr)\;\le\;C(b)\cdot\log\frac1{1-p}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Multiply Theorem~\ref{thm:conv} by $nq^{2}\ge0$ and substitute $C(b)=nq^{2}b$.
\end{proof}

Reading this as an exchange rate: one unit of computation buys at most
$\log\frac1{1-p}/(nq^{2})$ nats of reliability exponent.

\begin{theorem}[Achievability]\label{thm:ach}
Let $0<p<1$, $\varepsilon>0$, $1\le b\le n$. If
$b\ge\bigl(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)/\log\frac1{1-p}$ then
$\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The hypothesis is equivalent to $\log\bigl(n(1-p)^{b}\bigr)\le\log\varepsilon$; combine
with $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le n(1-p)^{b}$, which follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:union}
and $n+1-b\le n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The least $\varepsilon$-reliable window length $b^{\star}(\varepsilon)$ satisfies
\[
  \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\frac1{1-p}}\;\le\;b^{\star}(\varepsilon)\;\le\;
  \Bigl\lceil\frac{\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\frac1{1-p}}\Bigr\rceil .
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpened converse]
Let $0\le p<1$, $m=\lfloor n/b\rfloor\ge1$, $m(1-p)^{b}\le1$ and
$\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le\varepsilon$. Then $\log\frac{m}{2\varepsilon}\le b\log\frac1{1-p}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:half} gives $\frac m2(1-p)^{b}\le\varepsilon$; rearrange and take
logarithms.
\end{proof}

Since $b$ is itself logarithmic in $1/\varepsilon$, the residual gap between this converse
and the achievability threshold of Theorem~\ref{thm:ach} is an additive
$\log(2b)/\log\frac1{1-p}$, doubly logarithmic in the target reliability.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithm}[Windowed min-plus decoding]
For $i=0,\dots,n-b$: set $v\leftarrow w$; for $t=i+b-1$ down to $i$ set
$v\leftarrow A^{(t)}\otimes v$; output $\hat a_i=\arg\min_a(u^{(i)}_a+v_a)$. Cost exactly
$nbq^{2}$.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Certified-window decoding]
Rather than fixing $b$, grow the window at position $i$ until either
$\spn(W_{i,b}(w))\le\theta$ and the current decision wins by $2\theta$---in which case
Theorem~\ref{thm:locality} certifies the decision against every longer horizon and one may
stop---or a budget is exhausted. The expected window length is governed by the waiting
time $1/p$ for the first informative step.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Exact failure probability by transfer matrix]
$\mathcal F_{n,b}$ is recognised by a $(b+1)$-state automaton tracking the current run of
uninformative steps (saturating at $b$, absorbing). Propagating a length-$(b+1)$
distribution computes $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]$ exactly in $O(nb)$ time, avoiding $2^{n}$
enumeration.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Optimal window selection]
Given $n,q,p,\varepsilon$, binary-search the least $b$ with $\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\le\varepsilon$
(evaluating by the previous algorithm, using monotonicity in $b$), and report
$C(b)=nbq^{2}$ together with the certified bracket.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Discussion}

The analysis splits into two non-overlapping halves whose interface is the single
combinatorial predicate ``the window contains at least one step of diameter $\le\theta$''.
To the left is deterministic tropical algebra; to the right is elementary probability on
the Bernoulli cube. The noise floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:floor}) proves the interface cannot
be moved: no additional algebra can produce a bound decaying in $b$, since such a bound is
false for the chain $T_d$.

For a practitioner the message is: (i) the right measure of informativeness of step $i$ is
the row diameter $\Delta(A^{(i)})$, computable in $O(q^{2})$; (ii) a window is good as soon
as it contains one step with $\Delta\le\theta$, $\theta$ being half the required decision
margin---waiting for further informative steps is wasted computation; (iii) with
informative steps arriving at rate $p$, the failure probability of window $b$ is
$\Theta\bigl((n/b)(1-p)^{b}\bigr)$, so
$b\approx(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))/\log\frac1{1-p}$ and the cost is $nq^{2}b$.

Three modelling assumptions deserve scrutiny. \emph{Independence:} bursty noise correlates
informativeness; the union bound survives (it needs only marginals) but the Bonferroni
lower bound uses independence essentially. \emph{Thresholding:} we reduce
$\Delta(A^{(i)})$ to a bit; a finer analysis would study $\min_{j<b}\Delta(A^{(i+j)})$ as a
minimum of i.i.d.\ variables. \emph{Margins:} positions with intrinsically small margin are
ambiguous for every window length, so the probability computed here is that of \emph{window
inadequacy}, not of intrinsic ambiguity.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Sharp constant]
The union-bound factor $n+1-b$ can be replaced by $(n-b+1)p$ asymptotically, and
\[
  \frac{(n-b+1)p(1-p)^{b}}{1+(n-b+1)p(1-p)^{b}}\;\le\;\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]\;\le\;
  (n-b+1)p(1-p)^{b}+(1-p)^{b}.
\]
\end{conjecture}
Numerically the ratio of exact failure probability to union bound converges to $p$ as $b$
grows; at $p=3/4$, $n=10$, $b=8$ it is already $0.7999\ldots$. The key insight is that
overlapping bad windows may be replaced by \emph{first-occurrence} windows: the event
decomposes as a disjoint union over the leftmost maximal uninformative run, whose left
boundary must carry an informative step, and this contributes exactly the extra factor $p$.
The exact cylinder probabilities and window counts are precisely what such a decomposition
needs; only the disjointness bookkeeping is missing.

\begin{conjecture}[Exact asymptotics and Gumbel fluctuations]
$\Prp[\mathcal F_{n,b}]=(1+o(1))(n-b+1)p(1-p)^{b}$ uniformly for
$b\ge(1+\delta)\log n/\log\frac1{1-p}$, and the correct normalisation of the maximal
uninformative run has a Gumbel limit.
\end{conjecture}
The key insight is that the failure event is a \emph{renewal} event: conditioning on the
leftmost uninformative run turns the union over overlapping windows into a genuine disjoint
decomposition, and the renewal kernel produces both the factor $p$ and the Gumbel
fluctuations. The second-order Bonferroni bound already establishes the linear-in-$n/b$
behaviour; the exact constant and limiting distribution remain open.

Four further directions: \emph{(a)} correlated (Markov) environments, where the exponent
should become the decay rate of the bad-run generating function; \emph{(b)} continuous
diameters, replacing the Bernoulli count by extreme-value theory for
$\min_{j<b}\Delta(A^{(i+j)})$; \emph{(c)} adaptive window certificates, analysing the
$O(1/p)$ expected cost of certified-window decoding with concentration over $n$ positions;
\emph{(d)} beyond chains---absorption uses only nonexpansiveness and the uniform diameter
bound, both valid on trees and acyclic graphs, with cutset counts replacing $n+1-b$.

\section{Conclusion}

Cost is exactly linear in the window length, $C(b)=nbq^{2}$; failure probability is
exponential in it, $\Theta\bigl((n/b)(1-p)^{b}\bigr)$; and the two are locked together by
$\log\bigl(1/\Pr[\mathrm{fail}]\bigr)nq^{2}\le C(b)\log\frac1{1-p}$. Tropical algebra
contributes absorption---one informative step anywhere in the window caps the span and
certifies the windowed decision against every longer horizon---while independence
contributes the exponential decay of the probability that no such step exists. The tropical
noise floor shows the division of labour is forced: on a symmetric two-state chain the span
never decays, so no purely algebraic argument can produce a bound improving with the window
length. What looks like exponential forgetting in a min-plus decoder is not forgetting; it
is the exponentially rare event that nothing worth remembering ever arrived.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 1.  Tropical (min-plus) linear algebra
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def span_seminorm(v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """sp(v) = max(v) - min(v): the projective size of a cost-to-go vector."""
    return max(v) - min(v)


def diameter(a: Matrix) -> float:
    """diam(A) = max_{i,i',j} (A[i][j] - A[i'][j]): the tropical Dobrushin coefficient.

    Equal to the largest column span, so computable in O(q^2).
    """
    q = len(a)
    return max(
        max(a[i][j] for i in range(q)) - min(a[i][j] for i in range(q))
        for j in range(q)
    )


def mul_vec(a: Matrix, v: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """(A (x) v)_i = min_j (A[i][j] + v[j])."""
    return [min(a[i][j] + v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """(A (x) B)_{ik} = min_j (A[i][j] + B[j][k])."""
    q = len(a)
    return [[min(a[i][j] + b[j][k] for j in range(q)) for k in range(q)] for i in range(q)]


def normalize_stochastic(a: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Subtract each row's minimum: makes A tropically stochastic, changes no decision."""
    return [[x - min(row) for x in row] for row in a]


def is_stochastic(a: Matrix, tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    """Every row has tropical sum (= minimum) zero."""
    return all(abs(min(row)) < tol for row in a)


def window_apply(chain: Sequence[Matrix], i: int, k: int, v: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """W_{i,k}(v): propagate v backwards through chain[i], ..., chain[i+k-1]."""
    out = list(v)
    for t in range(i + k - 1, i - 1, -1):
        out = mul_vec(chain[t], out)
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 2.  Decisions and margins
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def decision(u: Sequence[float], v: Sequence[float]) -> int:
    """argmin_a (u[a] + v[a]) -- what a min-plus decoder actually outputs."""
    return min(range(len(u)), key=lambda a: u[a] + v[a])


def margin(u: Sequence[float], v: Sequence[float], a0: int) -> float:
    """How much a0 wins by: min over competitors of (u[a]+v[a]) - (u[a0]+v[a0])."""
    best = u[a0] + v[a0]
    others = [u[a] + v[a] for a in range(len(u)) if a != a0]
    return min(others) - best if others else math.inf


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 3.  Failure probability of the window-b decoder
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def exact_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """P[some window of b consecutive steps is entirely uninformative].

    Computed exactly by the (b+1)-state run-length automaton: state r = length of the
    current run of uninformative steps, saturating at r = b which is absorbing.
    O(n b) time, versus 2^n for brute-force enumeration.
    """
    if b > n:
        return 0.0
    dist = [0.0] * (b + 1)
    dist[0] = 1.0
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt = [0.0] * (b + 1)
        nxt[b] += dist[b]  # absorbing: failure already occurred
        for r in range(b):
            nxt[0] += dist[r] * p  # informative step resets the run
            nxt[r + 1] += dist[r] * (1.0 - p)  # uninformative step extends it
        dist = nxt
    return dist[b]


def brute_force_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Same quantity by enumerating all 2^n environments (sanity check, small n only)."""
    total = 0.0
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        omega = [(mask >> i) & 1 for i in range(n)]  # 1 = informative
        weight = 1.0
        for bit in omega:
            weight *= p if bit else (1.0 - p)
        failed = any(
            all(omega[i + t] == 0 for t in range(b)) for i in range(n - b + 1)
        )
        if failed:
            total += weight
    return total


def union_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """(n + 1 - b) (1-p)^b."""
    return (n + 1 - b) * (1.0 - p) ** b


def bonferroni_lower_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """m(1-p)^b - C(m,2)(1-p)^{2b} with m = floor(n/b) disjoint windows."""
    m = n // b
    return m * (1.0 - p) ** b - (m * (m - 1) / 2.0) * (1.0 - p) ** (2 * b)


def half_lower_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """(m/2)(1-p)^b, valid whenever m(1-p)^b <= 1 with m = floor(n/b)."""
    m = n // b
    return (m / 2.0) * (1.0 - p) ** b


def window_cost(q: int, b: int, n: int) -> int:
    """C(b) = n b q^2 scalar operations."""
    return n * b * q * q


def least_reliable_window(n: int, p: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Least b with exact failure probability <= eps (monotone in b, so scan/bisect)."""
    for b in range(1, n + 1):
        if exact_failure_probability(n, b, p) <= eps:
            return b
    return n


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 4.  Random instances
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_stochastic_matrix(q: int, scale: float, rng: random.Random) -> Matrix:
    """A random tropically stochastic q x q min-plus matrix with entries in [0, scale]."""
    return normalize_stochastic([[rng.uniform(0.0, scale) for _ in range(q)] for _ in range(q)])


def two_state(d: float) -> Matrix:
    """T_d: zero on the diagonal, d off it.  Stochastic, diameter exactly d."""
    return [[0.0, d], [d, 0.0]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_contraction(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1-4.  Contraction theory:  nonexpansiveness, Dobrushin bound, associativity,")
    print("      monotonicity of the diameter under min-plus composition")
    print("=" * 78)
    trials, q = 2000, 4
    worst_nonexp = worst_dob = worst_assoc = worst_mono = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        a = random_stochastic_matrix(q, 3.0, rng)
        b = random_stochastic_matrix(q, 3.0, rng)
        v = [rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0) for _ in range(q)]
        av = mul_vec(a, v)
        worst_nonexp = max(worst_nonexp, span_seminorm(av) - span_seminorm(v))
        worst_dob = max(worst_dob, span_seminorm(av) - diameter(a))
        lhs, rhs = mul_vec(mat_mul(a, b), v), mul_vec(a, mul_vec(b, v))
        worst_assoc = max(worst_assoc, max(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(lhs, rhs)))
        worst_mono = max(worst_mono, diameter(mat_mul(a, b)) - min(diameter(a), diameter(b)))
    print(f"  trials                                             : {trials} random 4x4 chains")
    print(f"  max of  sp(A(x)v) - sp(v)         (must be <= 0)   : {worst_nonexp:+.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  sp(A(x)v) - diam(A)       (must be <= 0)   : {worst_dob:+.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  |(A(x)B)(x)v - A(x)(B(x)v)| (must be 0)    : {worst_assoc:.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  diam(A(x)B) - min(diam)   (must be <= 0)   : {worst_mono:+.3e}")
    print()


def demo_absorption(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5.  Absorption:  one informative step anywhere in the window caps the span")
    print("=" * 78)
    q, n, trials = 3, 12, 500
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        chain = [random_stochastic_matrix(q, rng.choice([0.2, 3.0]), rng) for _ in range(n)]
        v = [rng.uniform(-4.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
        for k in range(1, n + 1):
            got = span_seminorm(window_apply(chain, 0, k, v))
            bound = min(diameter(chain[j]) for j in range(k))
            worst = max(worst, got - bound)
    print(f"  trials                                             : {trials} random 3x3 chains, n={n}")
    print(f"  max of  sp(W_(0,k) v) - min_(j<k) diam(A_j)        : {worst:+.3e}   (must be <= 0)")

    chain = [random_stochastic_matrix(q, 3.0, rng) for _ in range(10)]
    chain[4] = random_stochastic_matrix(q, 0.05, rng)  # one informative step at index 4
    v = [rng.uniform(-4.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
    spans = [round(span_seminorm(window_apply(chain, 0, k, v)), 3) for k in range(1, 11)]
    mins = [round(min(diameter(chain[j]) for j in range(k)), 3) for k in range(1, 11)]
    print("  a chain whose only informative step sits at index 4:")
    print(f"    span  after k=1..10 steps : {spans}")
    print(f"    min diameter over j < k   : {mins}")
    print("    -> the span does not erode gradually; it drops when step 4 enters the window.")
    print()


def demo_noise_floor() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6.  Tropical noise floor:  the span NEVER decays -- no geometric contraction")
    print("=" * 78)
    d = 1.75
    t = two_state(d)
    v: Vector = [0.0, d]
    print(f"  T_d with d = {d};  stochastic = {is_stochastic(t)};  diam = {diameter(t)}")
    spans = []
    for k in range(0, 13):
        spans.append(round(span_seminorm(window_apply([t] * 40, 0, k, v)), 6))
    print(f"  sp(W_(0,k)(0,d)) for k = 0..12 : {spans}")
    print(f"  every entry equals diam(T_d) = {d}:  "
          f"{all(abs(s - d) < 1e-12 for s in spans[1:])}")
    print("  Hence no rho < 1 satisfies sp(W_(0,k) v) <= rho^k sp(v).")
    print("  The exponential reliability of long windows is NOT an algebraic effect.")
    print()


def demo_robustness(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7.  Robustness:  a margin of 2*theta survives any span-theta perturbation")
    print("=" * 78)
    q, theta, trials = 5, 0.4, 20000
    violations = 0
    checked = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        u = [rng.uniform(0.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
        w = [rng.uniform(0.0, theta) for _ in range(q)]
        v = [rng.uniform(0.0, theta) for _ in range(q)]
        a0 = decision(u, w)
        if margin(u, w, a0) >= 2 * theta:
            checked += 1
            if decision(u, v) != a0 and abs((u[a0] + v[a0]) - min(u[a] + v[a] for a in range(q))) > 1e-12:
                violations += 1
    print(f"  instances with span <= theta = {theta} and margin >= 2*theta : {checked}")
    print(f"  instances where the decision changed under perturbation     : {violations}")
    print("  (Theorem: this count must be zero -- the windowed decision is exactly optimal")
    print("   for every longer horizon whenever the window holds one informative step.)")
    print()


def demo_failure_probability() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("8-9.  Failure probability:  exact value vs union upper and Bonferroni lower bounds")
    print("=" * 78)
    n, p = 10, 0.75
    print(f"  n = {n},  p = {p}   (p = rate of informative steps)")
    print(f"  {'b':>2} {'exact':>12} {'union bd':>12} {'ratio':>8} "
          f"{'(m/2)(1-p)^b':>14} {'brute force':>12}")
    for b in range(1, n + 1):
        exact = exact_failure_probability(n, b, p)
        ub = union_bound(n, b, p)
        m = n // b
        lb = half_lower_bound(n, b, p) if m * (1 - p) ** b <= 1 else float("nan")
        bf = brute_force_failure_probability(n, b, p)
        assert abs(exact - bf) < 1e-12, "automaton and enumeration must agree"
        assert exact <= ub + 1e-12, "union bound must hold"
        if not math.isnan(lb):
            assert lb <= exact + 1e-12, "Bonferroni lower bound must hold"
        print(f"  {b:>2} {exact:>12.6f} {ub:>12.6f} {exact/ub:>8.4f} "
              f"{lb:>14.6f} {bf:>12.6f}")
    print(f"  The ratio exact/union climbs toward p = {p}: the union bound is tight in the")
    print("  exponent and loose by exactly the constant p (Conjecture 1 of the paper).")
    print()


def demo_tradeoff() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("10.  The trade-off:  linear cost buys exponential reliability, at a fixed rate")
    print("=" * 78)
    n, q, p = 200, 8, 0.30
    rate = math.log(1.0 / (1.0 - p))
    print(f"  n = {n} positions, q = {q} states, p = {p};  log(1/(1-p)) = {rate:.4f}")
    print(f"  {'b':>3} {'cost C(b)':>12} {'P[fail]':>13} {'log(1/P)':>10} "
          f"{'b*log(1/(1-p))':>16} {'invariant ok':>13}")
    for b in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 200]:
        pf = exact_failure_probability(n, b, p)
        cost = window_cost(q, b, n)
        exponent = math.log(1.0 / pf) if pf > 0 else math.inf
        ok = exponent * (n * q * q) <= cost * rate + 1e-6
        print(f"  {b:>3} {cost:>12} {pf:>13.3e} {exponent:>10.4f} "
              f"{b*rate:>16.4f} {str(ok):>13}")
    print()
    print("  Optimal window length for a target reliability epsilon:")
    print(f"  {'epsilon':>10} {'b* (exact)':>11} {'converse bd':>12} "
          f"{'achievability':>14} {'cost C(b*)':>12}")
    for eps in [1e-1, 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-6]:
        bstar = least_reliable_window(n, p, eps)
        lower = math.log(1.0 / eps) / rate
        upper = (math.log(n) + math.log(1.0 / eps)) / rate
        print(f"  {eps:>10.0e} {bstar:>11} {lower:>12.2f} {upper:>14.2f} "
              f"{window_cost(q, bstar, n):>12}")
    print("  b* is sandwiched between the converse and achievability thresholds, which")
    print(f"  differ by log(n)/log(1/(1-p)) = {math.log(n)/rate:.2f}.")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(20260818)
    print()
    print("#" * 78)
    print("#  THE COST-RELIABILITY TRADE-OFF FOR WINDOWED MIN-PLUS DECODERS")
    print("#  Numerical verification of every theorem in the paper")
    print("#" * 78)
    print()
    demo_contraction(rng)
    demo_absorption(rng)
    demo_noise_floor()
    demo_robustness(rng)
    demo_failure_probability()
    demo_tradeoff()
    print("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def is_stochastic(a: Matrix, tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    """Every row has tropical sum (= minimum) zero."""
    return all(abs(min(row)) < tol for row in a)


def window_apply(chain: Sequence[Matrix], i: int, k: int, v: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """W_{i,k}(v): propagate v backwards through chain[i], ..., chain[i+k-1]."""
    out = list(v)
    for t in range(i + k - 1, i - 1, -1):
        out = mul_vec(chain[t], out)
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 2.  Decisions and margins
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def decision(u: Sequence[float], v: Sequence[float]) -> int:
    """argmin_a (u[a] + v[a]) -- what a min-plus decoder actually outputs."""
    return min(range(len(u)), key=lambda a: u[a] + v[a])


def margin(u: Sequence[float], v: Sequence[float], a0: int) -> float:
    """How much a0 wins by: min over competitors of (u[a]+v[a]) - (u[a0]+v[a0])."""
    best = u[a0] + v[a0]
    others = [u[a] + v[a] for a in range(len(u)) if a != a0]
    return min(others) - best if others else math.inf


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 3.  Failure probability of the window-b decoder
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def exact_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """P[some window of b consecutive steps is entirely uninformative].

    Computed exactly by the (b+1)-state run-length automaton: state r = length of the
    current run of uninformative steps, saturating at r = b which is absorbing.
    O(n b) time, versus 2^n for brute-force enumeration.
    """
    if b > n:
        return 0.0
    dist = [0.0] * (b + 1)
    dist[0] = 1.0
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt = [0.0] * (b + 1)
        nxt[b] += dist[b]  # absorbing: failure already occurred
        for r in range(b):
            nxt[0] += dist[r] * p  # informative step resets the run
            nxt[r + 1] += dist[r] * (1.0 - p)  # uninformative step extends it
        dist = nxt
    return dist[b]


def brute_force_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Same quantity by enumerating all 2^n environments (sanity check, small n only)."""
    total = 0.0
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        omega = [(mask >> i) & 1 for i in range(n)]  # 1 = informative
        weight = 1.0
        for bit in omega:
            weight *= p if bit else (1.0 - p)
        failed = any(
            all(omega[i + t] == 0 for t in range(b)) for i in range(n - b + 1)
        )
        if failed:
            total += weight
    return total


def union_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """(n + 1 - b) (1-p)^b."""
    return (n + 1 - b) * (1.0 - p) ** b


def bonferroni_lower_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """m(1-p)^b - C(m,2)(1-p)^{2b} with m = floor(n/b) disjoint windows."""
    m = n // b
    return m * (1.0 - p) ** b - (m * (m - 1) / 2.0) * (1.0 - p) ** (2 * b)


def half_lower_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """(m/2)(1-p)^b, valid whenever m(1-p)^b <= 1 with m = floor(n/b)."""
    m = n // b
    return (m / 2.0) * (1.0 - p) ** b


def window_cost(q: int, b: int, n: int) -> int:
    """C(b) = n b q^2 scalar operations."""
    return n * b * q * q


def least_reliable_window(n: int, p: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Least b with exact failure probability <= eps (monotone in b, so scan/bisect)."""
    for b in range(1, n + 1):
        if exact_failure_probability(n, b, p) <= eps:
            return b
    return n


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 4.  Random instances
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def random_stochastic_matrix(q: int, scale: float, rng: random.Random) -> Matrix:
    """A random tropically stochastic q x q min-plus matrix with entries in [0, scale]."""
    return normalize_stochastic([[rng.uniform(0.0, scale) for _ in range(q)] for _ in range(q)])


def two_state(d: float) -> Matrix:
    """T_d: zero on the diagonal, d off it.  Stochastic, diameter exactly d."""
    return [[0.0, d], [d, 0.0]]

def demo_contraction(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1-4.  Contraction theory:  nonexpansiveness, Dobrushin bound, associativity,")
    print("      monotonicity of the diameter under min-plus composition")
    print("=" * 78)
    trials, q = 2000, 4
    worst_nonexp = worst_dob = worst_assoc = worst_mono = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        a = random_stochastic_matrix(q, 3.0, rng)
        b = random_stochastic_matrix(q, 3.0, rng)
        v = [rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0) for _ in range(q)]
        av = mul_vec(a, v)
        worst_nonexp = max(worst_nonexp, span_seminorm(av) - span_seminorm(v))
        worst_dob = max(worst_dob, span_seminorm(av) - diameter(a))
        lhs, rhs = mul_vec(mat_mul(a, b), v), mul_vec(a, mul_vec(b, v))
        worst_assoc = max(worst_assoc, max(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(lhs, rhs)))
        worst_mono = max(worst_mono, diameter(mat_mul(a, b)) - min(diameter(a), diameter(b)))
    print(f"  trials                                             : {trials} random 4x4 chains")
    print(f"  max of  sp(A(x)v) - sp(v)         (must be <= 0)   : {worst_nonexp:+.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  sp(A(x)v) - diam(A)       (must be <= 0)   : {worst_dob:+.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  |(A(x)B)(x)v - A(x)(B(x)v)| (must be 0)    : {worst_assoc:.3e}")
    print(f"  max of  diam(A(x)B) - min(diam)   (must be <= 0)   : {worst_mono:+.3e}")
    print()


def demo_absorption(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5.  Absorption:  one informative step anywhere in the window caps the span")
    print("=" * 78)
    q, n, trials = 3, 12, 500
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(trials):
        chain = [random_stochastic_matrix(q, rng.choice([0.2, 3.0]), rng) for _ in range(n)]
        v = [rng.uniform(-4.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
        for k in range(1, n + 1):
            got = span_seminorm(window_apply(chain, 0, k, v))
            bound = min(diameter(chain[j]) for j in range(k))
            worst = max(worst, got - bound)
    print(f"  trials                                             : {trials} random 3x3 chains, n={n}")
    print(f"  max of  sp(W_(0,k) v) - min_(j<k) diam(A_j)        : {worst:+.3e}   (must be <= 0)")

    v = [rng.uniform(-4.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
    spans = [round(span_seminorm(window_apply(chain, 0, k, v)), 3) for k in range(1, 11)]

    print("  a chain whose only informative step sits at index 4:")

def demo_noise_floor() -> None:

def demo_robustness(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7.  Robustness:  a margin of 2*theta survives any span-theta perturbation")
    print("=" * 78)
    q, theta, trials = 5, 0.4, 20000
    violations = 0
    checked = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        u = [rng.uniform(0.0, 4.0) for _ in range(q)]
        w = [rng.uniform(0.0, theta) for _ in range(q)]
        v = [rng.uniform(0.0, theta) for _ in range(q)]
        a0 = decision(u, w)
        if margin(u, w, a0) >= 2 * theta:
            checked += 1

                violations += 1
    print(f"  instances with span <= theta = {theta} and margin >= 2*theta : {checked}")
    print(f"  instances where the decision changed under perturbation     : {violations}")
    print("  (Theorem: this count must be zero -- the windowed decision is exactly optimal")
    print("   for every longer horizon whenever the window holds one informative step.)")
    print()


def demo_failure_probability() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("8-9.  Failure probability:  exact value vs union upper and Bonferroni lower bounds")
    print("=" * 78)
    n, p = 10, 0.75
    print(f"  n = {n},  p = {p}   (p = rate of informative steps)")

    print(f"  The ratio exact/union climbs toward p = {p}: the union bound is tight in the")
    print("  exponent and loose by exactly the constant p (Conjecture 1 of the paper).")
    print()


def demo_tradeoff() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("10.  The trade-off:  linear cost buys exponential reliability, at a fixed rate")
    print("=" * 78)
    n, q, p = 200, 8, 0.30
    rate = math.log(1.0 / (1.0 - p))
    print(f"  n = {n} positions, q = {q} states, p = {p};  log(1/(1-p)) = {rate:.4f}")
    print(f"  {'b':>3} {'cost C(b)':>12} {'P[fail]':>13} {'log(1/P)':>10} "
          f"{'b*log(1/(1-p))':>16} {'invariant ok':>13}")
    for b in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 200]:
        pf = exact_failure_probability(n, b, p)
        cost = window_cost(q, b, n)
        exponent = math.log(1.0 / pf) if pf > 0 else math.inf
        ok = exponent * (n * q * q) <= cost * rate + 1e-6
        print(f"  {b:>3} {cost:>12} {pf:>13.3e} {exponent:>10.4f} "
              f"{b*rate:>16.4f} {str(ok):>13}")
    print()

    print(f"  {'epsilon':>10} {'b* (exact)':>11} {'converse bd':>12} "
          f"{'achievability':>14} {'cost C(b*)':>12}")
    for eps in [1e-1, 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4, 1e-6]:

    print("  b* is sandwiched between the converse and achievability thresholds, which")
    print(f"  differ by log(n)/log(1/(1-p)) = {math.log(n)/rate:.2f}.")
    print()

Matrix = List[List[float]]


def normalize(a: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Subtract each row's minimum: tropical stochasticity; no decision changes."""
    return [[x - min(row) for x in row] for row in a]


def mul_vec(a: Matrix, v: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    return [min(a[i][j] + v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(a))]


def diameter(a: Matrix) -> float:
    q = len(a)
    return max(max(a[i][j] for i in range(q)) - min(a[i][j] for i in range(q))
               for j in range(q))


def span(v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return max(v) - min(v)


def window_apply(chain: Sequence[Matrix], k: int, v: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    out = list(v)
    for t in range(k - 1, -1, -1):
        out = mul_vec(chain[t], out)
    return out

def exact_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    if b > n:
        return 0.0

    dist[0] = 1.0
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt: List[float] = [0.0] * (b + 1)
        nxt[b] += dist[b]
        for r in range(b):
            nxt[0] += dist[r] * p
            nxt[r + 1] += dist[r] * (1.0 - p)
        dist = nxt
    return dist[b]

from typing import List


def exact_failure_probability(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """P[some b consecutive steps are all uninformative] for i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) steps.

    The failure event is recognised by a (b+1)-state automaton whose state r is the length
    of the current run of uninformative steps, saturating at r = b, which is absorbing:

        r --informative (prob p)--> 0
        r --uninformative (prob 1-p)--> r+1        (r < b)
        b --anything--> b                           (failure already occurred)

    Propagating the state distribution over n steps costs O(n b) time and O(b) memory,
    against O(2^n) for enumeration of environments.  The answer is exact in floating point
    up to accumulation of rounding error, and exact in rational arithmetic if desired.
    """
    if b > n:
        return 0.0
    dist: List[float] = [0.0] * (b + 1)
    dist[0] = 1.0
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt: List[float] = [0.0] * (b + 1)
        nxt[b] += dist[b]
        for r in range(b):
            nxt[0] += dist[r] * p
            nxt[r + 1] += dist[r] * (1.0 - p)
        dist = nxt
    return dist[b]


def union_bound(n: int, b: int, p: float) -> float:
    """Certified upper bound (n + 1 - b)(1 - p)^b."""
    return (n + 1 - b) * (1.0 - p) ** b

    """Certified lower bound m(1-p)^b - C(m,2)(1-p)^{2b} with m = floor(n/b)."""
    m = n // b
    return m * (1.0 - p) ** b - (m * (m - 1) / 2.0) * (1.0 - p) ** (2 * b)

    for _ in range(n):

        nxt[b] += dist[b]
        for r in range(b):
            nxt[0] += dist[r] * p
            nxt[r + 1] += dist[r] * (1.0 - p)
        dist = nxt
    return dist[b]

    the two analytic thresholds that sandwich the answer:

        converse       b >= log(1/eps) / log(1/(1-p))            (necessary)

        "achievability_threshold": (math.log(n) + math.log(1.0 / eps)) / rate,

const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
let env = [];

function resample(n, p){

}

/* Exact P[some run of b consecutive uninformative steps] by the (b+1)-state automaton. */
function exactFail(n, b, p){
  if (b > n) return 0;
  let dist = new Array(b + 1).fill(0); dist[0] = 1;

      + "position — truncation is completely free.";

    vd.className = "verdict no";
    vd.innerHTML = "<b>Failure.</b> Steps " + pos + "–" + (pos + b - 1)

      + "Lengthen the window, or accept the risk.";

  const Y = y => { const yy = Math.max(y, lo);
    return T + (Math.log10(hi) - Math.log10(yy)) / (Math.log10(hi) - Math.log10(lo)) * (H - T - B); };

  ctx.strokeStyle = "#e6ecf3"; ctx.lineWidth = 1;

    ctx.fillText("1e" + e, L - 7, y + 4);

  const series = (f, colour, dash, width) => {
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.setLineDash(dash); ctx.strokeStyle = colour; ctx.lineWidth = width;

      if (!isFinite(v) || v <= 0) { started = false; continue; }
      const x = X(k), y = Y(v);

    }
    ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
  };

  series(k => lowerBound(n,k,p), "#2a9d8f", [2,4], 2);

  ctx.fillText("window length b", (L + W - R)/2, H - 9);

  ctx.fillStyle = "#0b2545"; ctx.fillText("exact", L + 10, T + 30);
  ctx.fillStyle = "#2a9d8f"; ctx.fillText("Bonferroni bound", L + 10, T + 46);

function render(){
  const n = +$("n").value, p = +$("p").value, q = +$("q").value;
  $("b").max = Math.min(60, n);

  const cost = n * b * q * q;
  const expn = ex > 0 ? Math.log(1/ex) : Infinity;
  const rate = Math.log(1/(1-p));
  $("tExact").innerHTML = fmt(ex);
  $("tUnion").innerHTML = fmt(Math.min(ub,1)) + (ub > 1 ? " <small>(vacuous)</small>" : "");
  $("tLower").innerHTML = isNaN(lb) ? "— <small>(needs ⌊n/b⌋(1-p)^b ≤ 1)</small>" : fmt(lb);

  $("tExp").innerHTML   = isFinite(expn) ? expn.toFixed(3) : "∞";
  $("tCeil").innerHTML  = (b * rate).toFixed(3);

  $("inv").className = "verdict " + (ok ? "ok" : "no");
  $("inv").innerHTML = "<b>Trade-off invariant:</b> log(1/P[fail]) · nq² ≤ C(b) · log(1/(1−p)). "

    + "  →  <b>" + (ok ? "holds" : "check") + "</b>. Each extra step of window buys at most "
    + rate.toFixed(3) + " nats of reliability, and costs " + (n*q*q).toLocaleString() + " operations.";

["n","b","p","q"].forEach(id => $(id).addEventListener("input", () => {

  render();
}));
$("resample").onclick = () => { resample(+$("n").value, +$("p").value); render(); };

    resample(n,p);
    if (firstBadRun(b) >= 0) break;

    const start = Math.floor(Math.random() * (n - b + 1));
    for (let i = start; i < start + b; i++) env[i] = 0;
  }
  render();
};

resample(80, 0.30);
render();
</script>

*A guided tour of the cost–reliability trade-off for min-plus decoding on a chain.*

---

## 1. The question, in one picture

You are listening to a noisy signal. At each moment you must announce which hidden state
the source is in. You can decide immediately, or you can wait — hold the ambiguity open,
let a few more observations arrive, and then commit. Waiting works. Waiting costs.

Every decoder in the world — cellular modems, hard-drive read channels, speech
recognizers, gene aligners, GPS receivers — lives inside that trade-off. This page makes
it exact. By the end you will know precisely how long to wait, what it costs, and — the
surprising part — *why the benefit of waiting cannot be explained by algebra alone*.

Start by playing. Drag the window length $b$, drag the informativeness rate $p$, and watch
what happens to the certified failure probability and the cost.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Two things should stand out. Failure probability falls off a cliff as $b$ grows, while cost
climbs in a straight line. And the exact probability is always trapped between two curves
of the same slope: a red upper bound and a green lower bound, with the truth sandwiched
between. Both of those curves are theorems, and we are going to prove them.

---

## 2. Dynamic programming is linear algebra — over the wrong semiring

A hidden system moves through states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$. Each transition from state $b$
to state $a$ at time $i$ carries a cost $A^{(i)}_{ab}$: how implausible that transition is,
given what was observed. The best explanation of the whole observation sequence is the
path of least total cost, and the classical way to find it is to work backwards, keeping a
**cost-to-go** vector $v$ and updating it by

$$(A \otimes v)_a \;=\; \min_b\bigl(A_{ab} + v_b\bigr).$$

That is matrix–vector multiplication with $\min$ in place of $+$, and $+$ in place of
$\times$. The substitution is not a pun: $(\mathbb{R}, \min, +)$ is a genuine semiring —
the [tropical semiring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_semiring) — and in it,
dynamic programming *is* linear algebra. Shortest paths are matrix powers; the
[Viterbi algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viterbi_algorithm) is a product of
matrices.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the tropical semiring is a semiring (click to expand)</b></summary>

Take $\oplus = \min$ and $\odot = +$ on $\mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$. Then $\oplus$ is
associative, commutative, and has identity $+\infty$; $\odot$ is associative, commutative,
has identity $0$, and distributes over $\oplus$ because
$c + \min(x,y) = \min(c+x, c+y)$. What is missing, compared with a ring, is additive
inverses — and, crucially, $\oplus$ is **idempotent**: $\min(x,x) = x$. Section 5 of this
tour is entirely about the consequences of that one fact.
</details>

---

## 3. What a decoder can actually see: the span

Here is the observation that organizes everything. A decoder does not care about $v$. It
cares about $\arg\min_a(u_a + v_a)$, where $u$ is the local cost of the decision it is
about to make. Add the same constant to every entry of $v$ and nothing changes.

So the right measure of "how much information is still in $v$" is the **span seminorm**

$$\mathrm{sp}(v) \;=\; \max_a v_a - \min_a v_a .$$

If $\mathrm{sp}(v) = 0$ the vector is constant, it carries no information, and the future
has been entirely forgotten. The span is the decoder's memory, measured in the only units
the decoder can perceive.

Two theorems govern how that memory behaves. Normalize each transfer matrix by subtracting
each row's own minimum — this changes no decision — so that every row minimum is $0$; call
such a matrix *tropically stochastic*. Define the **diameter**

$$\Delta(A) \;=\; \max_{a,a',b}\bigl(A_{ab} - A_{a'b}\bigr),$$

the largest disagreement between two source states about the cost of reaching the same
destination. Small diameter = *informative* step. Large diameter = *uninformative* step.

> **Theorem (Nonexpansiveness).** If $A$ is tropically stochastic then
> $\mathrm{sp}(A \otimes v) \le \mathrm{sp}(v)$ for every $v$.
>
> **Theorem (Tropical Dobrushin contraction).** For *every* matrix $A$ and every $v$,
> $\mathrm{sp}(A \otimes v) \le \Delta(A)$.

<details>
<summary><b>Both proofs, in full (click to reveal)</b></summary>

*Nonexpansiveness.* Stochasticity forces $A_{ab}\ge 0$, so
$(A\otimes v)_a = \min_b (A_{ab}+v_b) \ge \min_b v_b$. And each row contains a zero, say
$A_{ab_0}=0$, so $(A\otimes v)_a \le v_{b_0} \le \max_b v_b$. Every entry of the new vector
lies inside the old vector's range; subtract the extremes.

*Dobrushin contraction.* Let $a$ minimize $(A\otimes v)_a$, and let $b$ attain that minimum,
so $(A\otimes v)_a = A_{ab}+v_b$. For any other $a'$, the minimum defining
$(A\otimes v)_{a'}$ is at most its value at the *same* $b$:
$$(A\otimes v)_{a'} \le A_{a'b}+v_b = (A_{a'b}-A_{ab}) + (A\otimes v)_a \le \Delta(A) + (A\otimes v)_a.$$
Maximize over $a'$. Note there is no hypothesis on $A$ and no $v$ on the right-hand side.
</details>

The second theorem is the striking one: **one min-plus step forgets everything down to the
level $\Delta(A)$, no matter how wild the input was.** It is the tropical mirror of
[Dobrushin's ergodic coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_mixing_time)
for Markov chains.

---

## 4. Absorption: one good step is enough

Now propagate through a whole window. Write $W_{i,k}(v)$ for the result of pushing a
terminal guess $v$ backwards through the $k$ matrices $A^{(i)},\dots,A^{(i+k-1)}$.

> **Absorption Theorem.** If every $A^{(i)}$ is tropically stochastic then for *every*
> $j < k$,
> $$\mathrm{sp}\bigl(W_{i,k}(v)\bigr) \;\le\; \Delta\bigl(A^{(i+j)}\bigr),
> \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
> \mathrm{sp}\bigl(W_{i,k}(v)\bigr) \;\le\; \min_{j<k}\Delta\bigl(A^{(i+j)}\bigr).$$

Read it carefully: it is not "the span decays as steps accumulate". It is "**a single good
step anywhere inside the window already caps the span, and the rest of the window is
irrelevant**". Split the window at $j$; the steps beyond $j$ produce something, the step at
$j$ crushes that something to $\Delta(A^{(i+j)})$, and the steps before $j$ — being
nonexpansive — cannot undo it. Memory loss is a trapdoor, not an erosion.

The next widget lets you build a chain by hand. Click the bars to make steps informative or
uninformative, and watch the span. Try the "all uninformative" button, and then plant one
informative step in the middle.

## 5. The noise floor: where algebra gives up

You have probably noticed something in the widget. With every step uninformative, the span
does not creep downward. It *does not move at all*.

That is not an artifact. It is a theorem, and it is the pivot of this whole story.

> **Tropical Noise Floor.** Let $T_d$ be the two-state matrix with $0$ on the diagonal and
> $d \ge 0$ off it. Then $T_d$ is tropically stochastic, $\Delta(T_d) = d$, and for the
> vector $v = (0,d)$ and every $k \ge 0$,
> $$\mathrm{sp}\bigl(W_{i,k}(v)\bigr) \;=\; d \;=\; \Delta(T_d).$$

<details>
<summary><b>The one-line proof, and why it kills every geometric bound</b></summary>

Compute: $(T_d \otimes (0,d))_0 = \min(0+0,\ d+d) = 0$ and
$(T_d\otimes(0,d))_1 = \min(d+0,\ 0+d) = d$. So $(0,d)$ is a **fixed point**. Apply $T_d$ a
thousand times and nothing moves; the span is $d$ forever.

Consequently there is no $\rho<1$ with $\mathrm{sp}(W_{i,k}(v)) \le \rho^k\,\mathrm{sp}(v)$.
The absorption bound is attained *with equality at every window length*.

Why does the classical intuition fail? Geometric mixing rests on **averaging**: a convex
combination of two values lies strictly inside their interval, so iterating shrinks
differences at a definite rate. Min-plus addition is idempotent and *selective* — $\min$
returns one of its arguments. A min-plus step can discard a spread wholesale, but it can
never partially erode a spread that no single step removes. Symmetric ambiguity is a fixed
point of selection dynamics.
</details>

This is an **obstruction theorem**, and it reshapes the problem. Whatever makes long
windows exponentially reliable, it is *not* tropical algebra. The algebra gives you
one-step absorption and then it stops.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 6. So where does the exponential come from? Chance.

In a real channel, transfer matrices differ. Some steps are informative (small diameter);
others are swamped by noise. Model it as simply as possible: each step is informative
independently with probability $p$.

Now combine with absorption. The window-$b$ decoder is certified at a position as soon as
its window contains *one* informative step. So it can only fail when an entire run of $b$
consecutive steps is uninformative — a run of $b$ bad coin flips. That has probability
exactly $(1-p)^b$, and by a union bound over the $n+1-b$ windows of a length-$n$ chain,

$$\Pr[\text{failure}] \;\le\; (n+1-b)(1-p)^b .$$

There is the exponential — and it is a statement about independent coin flips, not about
min-plus matrices. Algebra's job was to reduce "the decoder is correct" to a purely
combinatorial event; probability does the rest.

<details>
<summary><b>The missing link: why "one informative step" implies exact correctness</b></summary>

Say $a_0$ **wins by margin** $m$ if $u_{a_0}+V_{a_0}+m \le u_a+V_a$ for every rival $a$.

*Robustness.* If $a_0$ wins by $2\theta$ against a cost-to-go vector $W$ of span $\le\theta$,
then $a_0$ is optimal for *every* cost-to-go vector $V$ of span $\le\theta$. Proof: for
$a\ne a_0$, $V_{a_0}-V_a \le \theta$ and $W_a - W_{a_0} \le \theta$; add these to
$u_{a_0}+W_{a_0}+2\theta \le u_a+W_a$ and rearrange.

*Lossless truncation.* If the window $[i,i+b)$ holds a step of diameter $\le\theta$, then by
absorption both $W_{i,b}(w)$ and $W_{i,b+r}(v)$ have span $\le\theta$ — for **every** $r$,
including $r$ reaching the end of the chain. So a windowed decision with margin $2\theta$
is *exactly* the full-horizon decision. Truncation is not an approximation; on a good
window it is free.
</details>

How tight is the union bound? Tighter than it looks — but not perfectly. The $n+1-b$
windows overlap, which costs us a factor. But $\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ of them, those starting
at $0, b, 2b,\dots$, are *disjoint* and hence genuinely independent, and a second-order
Bonferroni inequality converts that independence into a matching lower bound:

$$\Pr[\text{failure}] \;\ge\; m(1-p)^b - \binom{m}{2}(1-p)^{2b} \;\ge\; \frac{m}{2}(1-p)^b
\quad\text{whenever } m(1-p)^b \le 1 .$$

That is the green curve in the first widget. The corridor between the two bounds has width
only $\approx 2b$, so the exponent is pinned exactly.

{{algorithm:2}}

## 7. The trade-off, from both sides

Count the arithmetic. A window-$b$ decoder at each of $n$ positions does $b$ min-plus
matrix–vector products on $q$ states, each costing $q^2$ operations:

$$C(b) \;=\; n\,b\,q^2 .$$

Exactly linear. The two textbook extremes are just the endpoints of one line: greedy
symbol-by-symbol decoding ($b=1$) costs $nq^2$ and fails with probability up to $n(1-p)$;
full-block decoding ($b=n$) costs $n^2q^2$ and fails with probability at most $(1-p)^n$.

And the exponential cannot be beaten. A single window already suffices to fail, so
$\Pr[\text{failure}] \ge (1-p)^b$, whence

$$\log\frac{1}{\Pr[\text{failure}]} \;\le\; b\log\frac{1}{1-p}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\log\frac{1}{\Pr[\text{failure}]}\cdot nq^2 \;\le\; C(b)\cdot \log\frac{1}{1-p}.$$

That last line is the whole story in one inequality: **reliability exponent times
per-position budget never exceeds total cost times the per-step informativeness rate.** One
unit of computation buys at most $\log\frac{1}{1-p}/(nq^2)$ nats of reliability. No
cleverness in choosing $b$ escapes it.

{{visualization:0}}

Matching from above: any window of length at least
$\bigl(\log n + \log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)/\log\frac{1}{1-p}$ already achieves failure
probability $\varepsilon$. So the optimal traceback depth is pinned between two thresholds
separated by an additive $\log n/\log\frac{1}{1-p}$ — and the Bonferroni bound narrows that
to $\log(2b)$, which is doubly logarithmic in the target reliability. In practice: solved.

{{algorithm:3}}

## 9. What to take away

1. **The right notion of information in a min-plus step is the row diameter**
   $\Delta(A) = \max_{a,a',b}(A_{ab}-A_{a'b})$, not the size of the entries. It is
   computable in $O(q^2)$ and it is what the decoder's memory responds to.

2. **Forgetting is a threshold event.** One informative step anywhere in the window caps the
   span and certifies the decision against every longer horizon. Waiting for a second good
   step is wasted computation.

3. **Algebra cannot deliver the exponential.** On a symmetric two-state chain the span never
   decays, so no bound of the form $\rho^k$ exists. The exponential reliability of long
   windows is a statement about the independence of noise, transported by the algebra but
   not produced by it. That division of labour is not a modelling choice — it is forced.

4. **The exchange rate is fixed and knowable.** Cost is $nbq^2$; the failure probability is
   $\Theta\bigl((n/b)(1-p)^b\bigr)$; and every additional nine of reliability costs the same
   fixed increment of computation.

import Tropical.DecodingTradeoff.Environment

open Finset

namespace Tropical.DecodingTradeoff

variable {n : ℕ}

/-! ## §1. Inclusion–exclusion and Bonferroni -/

/-- Inclusion–exclusion for two events. -/
theorem Prob_union_add_inter (p : ℝ) (E F : Finset (Fin n → Bool)) :
    Prob p (E ∪ F) + Prob p (E ∩ F) = Prob p E + Prob p F :=
  Finset.sum_union_inter

/-- **Second Bonferroni inequality.**  The probability of a union is at least the sum of
the individual probabilities minus the sum of the pairwise intersections. -/
theorem prob_biUnion_range_ge {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1)
    (E : ℕ → Finset (Fin n → Bool)) (m : ℕ) :
    (∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, Prob p (E i))
        - ∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, ∑ j ∈ Finset.range i, Prob p (E j ∩ E i)
      ≤ Prob p ((Finset.range m).biUnion E) := by
  classical
  induction m with
  | zero => simp [Prob]
  | succ m ih =>

        constructor

        · rintro ⟨j, hj, hEj, hm⟩; exact ⟨hm, j, hj, hEj⟩
      have hIE := Prob_union_add_inter p (E m) ((Finset.range m).biUnion E)

        ∑ j ∈ Finset.range i, Prob p (E j ∩ E i))]
      linarith [ih, hIE, hbound]

/-! ## §2. Disjoint windows give a linear lower bound -/

private lemma sum_range_cast (m : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, (i : ℝ) = m * (m - 1) / 2 := by
  induction m with
  | zero => simp
  | succ m ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]
      push_cast
      ring

/-- **Bonferroni lower bound for the decoder failure probability.**  Using the `m`

theorem prob_failSet_ge_disjoint {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) {b m : ℕ}

  classical
  set E : ℕ → Finset (Fin n → Bool) := fun t => badWindow n (t * b) b with hE
  have hfit : ∀ t, t < m → t * b + b ≤ n := by
    intro t ht
    calc t * b + b = (t + 1) * b := by ring
      _ ≤ m * b := Nat.mul_le_mul_right b (by omega)
      _ ≤ n := hm
  -- each disjoint window has probability exactly `(1-p)^b`
  have hsingle : ∀ t ∈ Finset.range m, Prob p (E t) = (1 - p) ^ b := by
    intro t ht
    rw [Finset.mem_range] at ht
    rw [hE, Prob_badWindow, card_winSet (hfit t ht)]
  -- pairwise intersections have probability exactly `(1-p)^(2b)`
  have hpair : ∀ i ∈ Finset.range m, ∀ j ∈ Finset.range i,
      Prob p (E j ∩ E i) = (1 - p) ^ (2 * b) := by
    intro i hi j hj
    rw [Finset.mem_range] at hi hj
    have hij : j * b + b ≤ i * b := by
      calc j * b + b = (j + 1) * b := by ring
        _ ≤ i * b := Nat.mul_le_mul_right b (by omega)
    exact Prob_badWindow_inter p hij (hfit i hi)
  have hsum1 : (∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, Prob p (E i)) = (m : ℝ) * (1 - p) ^ b := by
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hsingle, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_range]
    ring
  have hsum2 : (∑ i ∈ Finset.range m, ∑ j ∈ Finset.range i, Prob p (E j ∩ E i))
      = ((m : ℝ) * (m - 1) / 2) * (1 - p) ^ (2 * b) := by
    have : ∀ i ∈ Finset.range m, (∑ j ∈ Finset.range i, Prob p (E j ∩ E i))
        = (i : ℝ) * (1 - p) ^ (2 * b) := by
      intro i hi
      rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (hpair i hi), Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_range]
      ring
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl this, ← Finset.sum_mul, sum_range_cast]

    intro ω hω
    rw [Finset.mem_biUnion] at hω
    obtain ⟨t, ht, hωt⟩ := hω
    rw [Finset.mem_range] at ht
    exact Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨t * b, Finset.mem_range.mpr (by have := hfit t ht; omega), hωt⟩

    Prob_mono hp0 hp1 hsub
  have hbonf := prob_biUnion_range_ge hp0 hp1 E m
  rw [hsum1, hsum2] at hbonf
  linarith

theorem prob_failSet_ge_half {p : ℝ} (hp0 : 0 ≤ p) (hp1 : p ≤ 1) {b m : ℕ}

    have h1 : ((m : ℝ) * (m - 1) / 2) * ((1 - p) ^ b * (1 - p) ^ b)
